title: 2 Chronicles 34:14–28
context: During the temple repairs Hilkiah finds the book of the LORD’s law given by Moses. When it is read to Josiah he tears his clothes and sends officials to the prophetess Huldah, who confirms the coming judgment but promises that Josiah will be gathered to his grave in peace before it falls (compare 2 Kings 22:8–20).

verses.text: When they brought out the money that was brought into the LORD’s house, Hilkiah the priest found the book of the LORD’s law given by Moses.
verses.arminianNotes: As they bring out the money, “Hilkiah the priest found the book of the LORD’s law given by Moses.” Arminian readers see the rediscovery of God’s word as a turning point.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s word recovered at a crucial time. The Chronicler’s phrase “given by Moses” is more explicit than 2 Kings 22:8, and many identify the book with Deuteronomy or part of it, though the text does not say so.

verses.text: Hilkiah answered Shaphan the scribe, “I have found the book of the law in the LORD’s house.” So Hilkiah delivered the book to Shaphan.
verses.arminianNotes: Hilkiah says, “I have found the book of the law in the LORD’s house.” Arminian readers see the priest sharing the discovery promptly with the king’s scribe.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the word passed on faithfully. The wording matches the report in 2 Kings 22:8 and begins the chain of events leading to Josiah’s covenant.

verses.text: Shaphan carried the book to the king, and moreover brought back word to the king, saying, “All that was committed to your servants, they are doing.
verses.arminianNotes: Shaphan brings the book to the king and reports, “All that was committed to your servants, they are doing.” Arminian readers see faithful service reported before the remarkable news.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the ordinary placed before the extraordinary. The report confirms that the repair work was proceeding as commanded.

verses.text: They have emptied out the money that was found in the LORD’s house, and have delivered it into the hand of the overseers and into the hand of the workmen.”
verses.arminianNotes: “They have emptied out the money that was found in the LORD’s house.” Arminian readers see honest accounting of resources given for God’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the report of faithful administration. The detail parallels 2 Kings 22:9 and keeps the narrative grounded in the practical work of restoration.

verses.text: Shaphan the scribe told the king, saying, “Hilkiah the priest has delivered me a book.” Shaphan read from it to the king.
verses.arminianNotes: Shaphan says, “Hilkiah the priest has delivered me a book,” and reads from it to the king. Arminian readers see God’s word reaching the king through faithful servants.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the word read before the king. The understated introduction contrasts with the profound effect the book will have.

verses.text: When the king had heard the words of the law, he tore his clothes.
verses.arminianNotes: “When the king had heard the words of the law, he tore his clothes.” Arminian readers see a heart responding to God’s word with humility and grief.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the word producing conviction. As with 2 Kings 22:11, readers in both traditions commonly treat this response as a model of receiving God’s word seriously.

verses.text: The king commanded Hilkiah, Ahikam the son of Shaphan, Abdon the son of Micah, Shaphan the scribe, and Asaiah the king’s servant, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The king commands Hilkiah, Ahikam, Abdon, Shaphan, and Asaiah. Arminian readers see Josiah acting immediately on his conviction, involving trusted leaders.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the king’s urgency. The Chronicler names “Abdon the son of Micah” where 2 Kings 22:12 has Achbor son of Micaiah, a difference noted rather than harmonized.

verses.text: “Go inquire of the LORD for me, and for those who are left in Israel and in Judah, concerning the words of the book that is found; for great is the LORD’s wrath that is poured out on us, because our fathers have not kept the LORD’s word, to do according to all that is written in this book.”
verses.arminianNotes: Josiah says, “Go inquire of the LORD for me, and for those who are left in Israel and in Judah.” Arminian readers see the king confessing inherited guilt and seeking God for the whole people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Josiah acknowledging that “our fathers have not kept the LORD’s word.” The phrase “those who are left in Israel” reflects the Chronicler’s concern for the remnant of the north.

verses.text: So Hilkiah and those whom the king had commanded went to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tokhath, the son of Hasrah, keeper of the wardrobe (now she lived in Jerusalem in the second quarter), and they spoke to her to that effect.
verses.arminianNotes: The officials go to Huldah the prophetess in Jerusalem’s second quarter. Arminian readers see God speaking through a woman prophet whom the king’s officials recognize as authoritative.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Huldah consulted as a true prophet. Her family names differ slightly from 2 Kings 22:14, and readers in this tradition note the variation without pressing it.

verses.text: She said to them, “The LORD, the God of Israel says: ‘Tell the man who sent you to me,
verses.arminianNotes: She says, “The LORD, the God of Israel says: ‘Tell the man who sent you to me.’” Arminian readers see Huldah speaking with divine authority to the king’s representatives.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Huldah delivering God’s word without hesitation. Her opening formula marks her message as the LORD’s, not her own opinion.

verses.text: “The LORD says, ‘Behold, I will bring evil on this place and on its inhabitants, even all the curses that are written in the book which they have read before the king of Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: “Behold, I will bring evil on this place … even all the curses that are written in the book.” Arminian readers see God confirming the warnings written in the book.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God affirming that his word will be fulfilled. The Chronicler’s mention of “all the curses” makes explicit what 2 Kings 22:16 calls “all the words of the book.”

verses.text: Because they have forsaken me, and have burned incense to other gods, that they might provoke me to anger with all the works of their hands, therefore my wrath is poured out on this place, and it will not be quenched.’ ” ’
verses.arminianNotes: “Because they have forsaken me, and have burned incense to other gods … my wrath is poured out on this place, and it will not be quenched.” Arminian readers see judgment grounded in persistent idolatry.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s wrath as his just response to idolatry. Readers in this tradition treat the verse, as in 2 Kings 22:17, as shared ground on the seriousness of covenant warnings.

verses.text: But to the king of Judah, who sent you to inquire of the LORD, you shall tell him this, ‘The LORD, the God of Israel says: “About the words which you have heard,
verses.arminianNotes: To the king who inquired, Huldah sends a separate word. Arminian readers see God distinguishing the king’s humble response from the nation’s rebellion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God addressing Josiah personally. The shift from the people to the king highlights how God regards those who humble themselves before his word.

verses.text: because your heart was tender, and you humbled yourself before God when you heard his words against this place and against its inhabitants, and have humbled yourself before me, and have torn your clothes and wept before me, I also have heard you,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “… because your heart was tender, and you humbled yourself before God … I also have heard you.” Arminian readers see God responding to Josiah’s humble repentance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God honoring a tender heart, which many in this tradition regard as itself a work of God’s grace. As in the 2 Kings 22:19 notes, this is shared ground on repentance under the word.

verses.text: “Behold, I will gather you to your fathers, and you will be gathered to your grave in peace. Your eyes won’t see all the evil that I will bring on this place and on its inhabitants.” ’ ” They brought back this message to the king.
verses.arminianNotes: “… you will be gathered to your grave in peace. Your eyes won’t see all the evil that I will bring on this place.” Arminian readers see mercy shown to Josiah in sparing him the coming disaster.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s kindness to Josiah. Readers in this tradition commonly understand “in peace” as dying before the catastrophe, as in the 2 Kings 22:20 notes.
